rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: Two of your relatives, the saltwater crocodile and the freshwater crocodile, have a streak of sharpest vision that runs across the back of each eye from the nose side to the temple side. At its best the saltwater crocodile sees about 9 cycles a degree, less than a third of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured where your sharpest spot lies or how sharply you see.
rows.note: Records cover only Crocodylus species; nothing for Alligator, so the row stays at i.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are an American alligator, the cone cells in your eyes hold four kinds of light-sensing pigment, where a human has three. One of them sits in a single cone and senses light most strongly at 535 nanometers. If you are a saltwater crocodile, your three kinds of single cone sense violet, green and red light most strongly.
rows.note: Only one of the alligator's four pigment peaks is recorded (535 nm), so the others are left out. Caimans and most crocodiles are not covered by this row.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are an American alligator, the dark opening in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a China alligator, you very likely have the same, since your close relative the American alligator does. Among crocodiles, the saltwater crocodile has a vertical, mobile slit pupil, and nobody has measured the pupil shape of the other crocodiles, the caimans or the gharial.
rows.note: Removed the word "report". Caiman, gharial and most crocodile species have no pupil record, so the row says nobody has measured them.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness, dim light and depth
rows.text: Nobody has measured how wide you see, how sharply you see, how little light you need, or how you judge distance. Crocodilians have a reflecting layer in the eye for night vision, and in the saltwater crocodile it is brightest behind a furrowed slit, so you very likely have one as well. The only sharpness figure comes from the saltwater crocodile, about 9 cycles a degree against a human's 30, and in six crocodilian species the eyes were well focused in air for distant targets and severely defocused underwater.
rows.note: No record measures the American alligator itself for any of these traits; the sharpness figure is kept with the saltwater crocodile, and R4 does not list which six species were tested.
